## Paper 5 · Session 06 · India's tariff cuts and firm productivity {.center .scrollable}

## The paper, and its question {.scrollable}

**Topalova & Khandelwal (2011)**, *Trade liberalization and firm productivity: the case of India*,
Review of Economics and Statistics · [article](https://doi.org/10.1162/REST_a_00095)

In 1991 India cut its tariffs sharply because an IMF programme required it — not because some
industries asked. The authors follow about 3,000 listed firms and separate two channels: lower
tariffs on a firm's **output** (more competition) and on its **inputs** (cheaper intermediates).

> **Do lower output and input tariffs go with higher firm productivity?**

::: {.muted}
The paper compares each firm with itself before and after its tariffs fell, and finds that a
10-point cut in input tariffs raises productivity by about 4.8%. You fit the simpler regressions.
:::

## The data, and the simple models {.scrollable}

**14,648 firm-years, 3,077 firms, 1989–1996.** Outcome `tfp1000`: log productivity, so 100 × a
slope is a percentage.

| Step | Model | Session |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | load, keep the paper's years, average tariffs by year | 02 |
| 2 | OLS: productivity on the output tariff — the slope in units | 03 |
| 3 | + the input tariff — "controlling for" | 03 |
| 4 | + ownership, size, age and year dummies `C(yr)` | 03 |
| 5 | + age squared — is the effect of age a curve? | 06 |
| 6 | side by side with the paper | — |

{{< include _solutions-r5.qmd >}}

## What you should find {.scrollable}

| | output tariff | input tariff |
|---|---|---|
| step 2 · tariff alone | −0.083 | — |
| step 3 · both tariffs | −0.066 | −0.075 |
| step 5 · + controls, year dummies, age² | −0.011 | +0.060 |
| paper · same firm over time | −0.032 | **−0.480** |

::: {.check}
Step 2: a 10-point output-tariff cut goes with 0.8% higher productivity. With year dummies the
slopes collapse: most of it was the common fall over time. Step 5 is exactly the paper's own
column 1 — where the authors *start*. Age: about −0.2% per year when young, −0.1% at 40.
:::

## What it does not license {.scrollable}

::: {.tight}
- **Different comparisons, different answers.** Your regressions compare *different firms*; the paper
  compares *each firm with itself*, so everything constant about a firm drops out. That is why its
  input effect is −0.48 and yours is near zero.
- **No "tariffs do not matter" from step 4.** A comparison across firms that cannot see the effect
  is not evidence of no effect.
- **No claim beyond surviving, listed manufacturing firms** — and productivity is itself an estimate.
:::
